In this paper, we introduce and analyze a new challenge involving task allocation and synchronization for a multi-task execution model. In this framework, each individual task possesses a specified start and end time, yet the endpoints are flexible within certain intervals. We address the challenge of coordinating multiple robots so that they successfully execute an assigned subset of these tasks. We define the "temporal flexibility" associated with any given schedule and demonstrate that increasing this flexibility necessarily requires a rise in total execution cost. Consequently, we construct a novel algorithm aimed at minimizing cost while maximizing temporal flexibility. This algorithm encompasses both "unbounded" and "bounded" variants, respectively allowing or restricting tasks to be executed outside their designated windows by some degree. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate key findings and validate the proposed methods.

Federized learning (FL) serves as an essential tool for collaboratively developing machine model while upholding data privacy. With the rising adoption of vertical federated learning (VFL)--where participating parties possess non-overlapping portions of columns within a shared entity entity entity entity--it has become increasingly crucial to assess and mitigate privacy risks associated with this approach in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce several practical attack methods designed to compromise VFL by reconstructing individual user data through collaborative inference. Specifically, we propose attacks leveraging both differential privacy (DPS) and synthetic data generation. Furthermore, these attacks effectively overcome common defenses, thereby raising significant privacy concerns for practical deployments of FFL.

Neural networks, when paired with carefully chosen kernel functions, have shown remarkable success in a broad spectrum of tasks. Our method employs a novel PRRF (our own dynamic RFF) that utilizes gradient information to refine kernel parameters during the learning process. The stability characteristics and educational application of this approach represent another area of exploration. Extensive experiments across various data sets demonstrate that this technique outperforms both traditional and existing R&F-based methods. Additionally, we investigate the potential use of this model in a practical educational context to facilitate student learning.

However, high-resolution simulations of disks affected by the vertical shear instability (VSI) reveal that VSI-triggered features extend not only in the gas density but also across multiple disk scales, appearing prominently at the observed continuums wavelengths. If this hypothesis is accurate, the unique capability of ALMA to observe at multiple frequencies allows us to directly verify the frequency-dependent merging characteristics of VSI patterns formed due to the vertical shear of the fluid. We therefore analyze a range of solutions with varying parameters to directly observe their features and produce synthetic data for modern observations with high accuracy and resolution. Our results show long-lived, spatially widely visible substructures in the dust emission with high intensity. We further predict prominent deviations from the standard thermal emission disk expectations, characterized by both low and erratic temperature variations. The results imply distinct signatures that are observable and directly testable with next generation instruments and methods, allowing us to differentiate disks regulated by the VSI from those shaped by planet formation activities.

Recent measurements of the ground states for calcium (Ca) isotopes reveal a significant curvature in their binding energies regarding nucleon number, exceeding predictions from standard semi-empirical formulas. This finding underscores the necessity for refined nuclear effective field theories that accurately incorporate shell evolution, competitive orbital configurations, and three-nucleon interactions. Despite this progress, existing frameworks fail to explain the exceptional surface properties of medium-weight apple-shaped nuclei, characterized by pronounced shell effects at their cores. While future experiments will be vital for testing these exotic atomic structures in nature, similar surface anomalies could also manifest more immediately within exotic nuclei of moderate mass.

This study presents the design and experimental verification of two-photon, frequency-stable Mølmer–Sørensen gates suitable for three motional degrees of freedom within a three-frequency ion trap. These gates are constructed so that two light sidebands, separated by the carrier frequency, interact coherly with either an ion's internal states or its collective motion. By utilizing the simplest pulshing waveform—a sinusoidal signal of constant amplitude—the operational fidelity of these gates remains largely unaffected by variations in the carrier frequency. Despite nominal hardware limitations and uncalibrated disturbances, these fluctuations have been compensated for, yielding gate fidelities exceeding 99.6\% across diverse settings in recent tests involving degrees of freedom. These results signify a crucial advancement toward utilizing entangling logic gates in quantum computations that rely on motional ancillae.

Although neural network-based language models have largely surpassed $n$-gram approaches in accuracy, this paper argues that discarding the latter was premature precision. We introduce a novel hybrid $n$-gram neural (NGN) framework that integrates the global contextual representation of neural models with the structural and syntactical grounding of $n$-grams to address the inherent short-term forgetfulness of standalone neural models. Experimental results demonstrate that NGN significantly outperforms pure neural baselines on both Chinese and English datasets, yielding approximately a 0.5 improvement in CER for Chinese text and roughly a 10% gain in word-level editing tasks for English text; furthermore, training times match those of pure neural models, while inference is just marginally more complex, confirming that abandoning $n$-gram approaches was unnecessary.

Recent advancements highlight a paradoxical trend in statistical learning where frameworks, despite exhibiting a lack of strict generalization bounds, actually deliver superior performance across various contexts. This paper investigates this phenomenon within time-series regression models using parameter dimensions $p$ that grow with the sample count $n$. In this setup (benign overfitting), the estimator fits noise in the most recent data points while predicting future values without strict generalization guarantees. The article explores the impact of different modeling techniques—specifically comparing standard methods against state-of-the-art orthogonal methods—on prediction precision. Conducted examinations, both through theoretical analysis in theoretical frameworks and practical tests using reliable data, reveal that moderate overparameterization yields benign results, whereas excessive parameters lead to benign outcomes where high-dimensional estimates remain precise.

We analyze a storage acquisition model within a decentralized environment where an agent with risk-averse preferences manages self-allocation. This agent interacts with a collection of suppliers, whose individual storage provision costs remain random and private. The entity determines both the quantity of storage to procure and the allocation amounts from each source by navigating this model through maximization of expected utility. We offer several insights derived from precise expressions of the self-allocation strategy for risk-averse agents, highlighting key characteristics regarding the impact of supply variability, risk tolerance levels, and the degree of risk sharing. Furthermore, we examine a competitive scenario involving many providers with uncorrelated cost fluctuations to investigate asymptotic behavior in this context.

We investigated atmospheric circulations in a 2D global model under various heating schemes, surface friction rules, and planetary rotation rates. Our primary goal was a qualitative examination of circulation patterns across the transition from rapid (cyclostrophic) super-rotation in highly rotated scenarios to geostrophic turbulence under weak rotation. While a single critical rotation rate theoretically separates these two behaviors in idealized cases, actual transitions occur over a broader range influenced by thermal forcing characteristics and surface drag rules. Drifting zonal jets appear as a common intermediate state between the two extremes. In terms of heat transport efficiency, cyclostrophic super-rotation under high rotation rates exhibits significantly lower efficiency compared to the more efficient geostrophic turbulence under low rotation rates.

This study addresses the challenge of learning multivariate functions with their derivatives integrated, utilizing an approach rooted in the differential equation solutions offered by Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs). By leveraging the preservation of the symplectic manifold structure during dynamics evolution, the method leverages both gradients and Hessian data to train on multivariate datasets, enabling the exploration of data geometry through symplectic manifolds even with limited samples. Although the framework supports broader applications such as various symplectic integration schemes and parameter-dependent Hamiltonians, the work focuses specifically on using Graduated Non-convex Optimization (GNO) to train on multi-variate regression tasks where gradients and Hessians are available, demonstrating its potential through three practical cases: a Hamiltonian for a specific physical system, parameter-dependent quantum circuit simulation, and controlling a quadrotor. The findings reveal high accuracy in estimating target functions, with derived gradient and Hessian estimates exhibiting exceptional fidelity.

MAJORScore introduces a highly innovative and valuable approach to enhancing MAHOML (a leading black-box sentiment analyzer) by prioritizing human input. It employs a competitive, pairwise comparison mechanism—resembling a sports tournament—where an user is presented with pairs of predictions, one enhanced and one unenhanced, until a clear winner emerges. The winning choice becomes a benchmark, and the process continues as new instances are pitted against it to identify a single most preferred output from multiple options. Though conceptually similar in structure to methods used for MAHOML comparison, this approach stands out due to its use of trust scores to guide enhancements and its reliance on specific data augmentation techniques curated by a single user. Distinctively, the proof-concept phase focuses exclusively on enhancing MAHOML sans access to a specific dataset for preliminary validation. While the paper posits clear avenues for future investigation, it acknowledges the absence of exploration into scalable human involvement in production environments and other refinable aspects of the proposed system. Ultimately, as posited in prior research posits that human-centered methodologies are essential for the practical application of automated solutions like MAHOML to achieve higher reliability and efficacy.

We construct a constructive quantum group theoretical invariant specifically for links situated within the thickened two-torus ($T^2 \times I$). This invariant demonstrates an asymptotic expansion as the parameter of quantization approaches the classical limit. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) addresses the challenge determining the specific meaning function of context-dependent words. Since a significant portion of a word's semantics often resides in its broader information not explicitly available in a particular context, this paper introduces a new method called Context-gloss Enhancement (CGE) to WSD that systematically and manually enriches contextualized words with their corresponding definitions taken from wordlist resources such as Wiktionary and Wikipedia. By integrating this CGE definition feature into various existing WSD models, we observe clear enhancements in both standalone and document-level disambiguation tasks. We present results indicating the detection of proton-nucleus (pA) top quark pair (t$\bar{\text{T}}$) production, derived from lead-lead (PbPb) data via an approach utilizing proton-proton (pp) information extracted within the pp invariant emission source method applied to PbPb datasets. The primary limitation in achieving such measurements within pA datasets—the scarce occurrence of top quark production— is effectively overcome. We observe a non-negligible top quark production rate in the sample of approximately 30,000 hadronized pairs migrated from pp events, migrated into what appears to be ~20 million hadronization events involving proton-nucleus collisions. Consequently, while we cannot yet claim a fully independent top quark production measurement in proton-nucleus collisions, we have successfully confirmed its presence with strong indicative evidence.

Hydrodynamic descriptions provide a useful bridge between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic behavior, though traditional approaches like those by Fluid QFT often hide microscopic intricacies and prove difficult to integrate with high-precision numerical methods. This work introduces "Phase-Space Random Quantum Hydro" (PS-RQH) as an innovative framework that preserves the detailed microstate features of fluid QFT while avoiding the use of heavy fields. Central to PS-RQH are Nonequilibrium Quantum Phase-Space Distribution Functions (NQPSDFs), which evolve according to coupled Wigner-Husimi equations. Because these functions exhibit stochastic intrinsic characteristics, they enable the application of advanced techniques from random field theory. Through perturbation analysis of the boson Hamiltonian in the low-density limit, we develop PS-RQH by expanding both quantum expectation values and stochastic PSDFs; this yields closed equations for quantum hydro dynamics at order $\alpha^{2,3}$ (for density and $8,6$ for density). Furthermore, we initiated a comparison between these new findings and molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate their utility.

The Ni isotopes have been a primary focus in the research on shape changes within the medium-mass mass region. In specific cases, such as 64Ni, experimental data indicates that shape coexistence exists among low-lying, zero-spin states. The current study applies an extensive 64n nucleon force, carefully parameterized to reproduce the energies of shell-model states observed experimentally, with the goal of identifying key features influencing this phenomenon. Variability in performance evaluations is a prevalent challenge for many natural language model architectures, stemming significantly in part from data leakage issues. While variations in traditional cross-validation setups contribute somewhat to this instability, it remains unclear whether cross-validation strategies utilizing re-sampling methods—such as K-fold—introduce additional variance, particularly in cross-language modeling scenarios where we seek to prevent the test language from appearing in training or validation folds. This study examines the impact of different NLP data set partitioning strategies to determine which approaches best minimize variance in performance evaluation, specifically investigating whether J-K fold cross-validation offers superior results compared to standard K-fold methods by ensuring no potentially overlapping data exists between any training, validation, or test partitions. Our empirical findings demonstrate that J-K fold cross-validation is indeed the superior strategy. Furthermore, in multilingual tasks where one must guarantee no test language contaminates the training or validation folds, J-K fold validation stands out as the most effective method for optimizing model performance tuning.

Finally, prospective N-I scenarios for future work are identified, encompassing topics such as Web Question Answering (WQA), Machine Translation (MT), Summary Generation (SUM), Dialogue Systems (DS), and human-interaction DNNs.

These issues are addressed: developing a new rapid four-dimensional (four directions in three spatial plus respiration) T2 turbo spin one with slice interleaving for continuous motion correction without requiring subject cooperation in breathing. This novel sequence reduces scanning time significantly by reducing data acquisition in three dimensions from two three-dimensional volumes, collecting it over a free breathing cycle. This study investigates the direction-dependent variation of drag forces experienced by cylindrical bodies moving through granular beds saturated with fluid. Discretization methods for time-evolving partial differential equations often need to maintain specific properties, like preserving symmetry or other characteristics inherent in the continuous system. Non-rigid alignment serves as a fundamental step in many medical analysis pipelines by registering non-rigid volumes to rigid surfaces. This paper presents a novel non-rigid registration method grounded in a data-driven biomechanical framework. Directly fitting this CTM to volumetric data allows it to capture structural characteristics while maintaining flexibility. Because CTM parameters vary locally, they can be efficiently optimized using a hybrid search strategy combining coarsely sampled jumps with gradient-descent refinement. Ultimately, this approach achieves high-accuracy non-rigid alignment between free-hand 3D ultrasonic volumes and corresponding organ surfaces, demonstrated here for fetal heart ultrasound guidance systems.

Color image demosaicing utilizes spatial multiplexing, allowing a color filter array (CMA) to lower hardware costs in image sensors; however, it requires complex post-processing to reconstruct missing values (demosaicing) to generate a full image. Conversely, color video compressive sensing achieves hardware reductions by randomly sampling green, red, and blue channels at specific spatio-temporal coordinates during image sensor exposure, thus capturing only two color components and generating data that is both spatially and temporally incomplete. The study proposes an innovative application of the learned unrolled operator (U-UO) within this compressive sensing video acquisition framework. Furthermore, the method is extended to enhance existing demosaicing capabilities for video and audio in color images. These advancements were validated on natural scenes and synthetic/computed datasets, using comparisons against current state-of-the-art models to verify the utility of these non-stationary techniques with fixed parameters, requiring no additional learning or adaptation. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate that optimizing code design paired with un-UO enhances performance across multiple data streams in color image demosaicing, at the added advantage of requiring training data only for the filter design parameters, which remain constant regardless of the specific application used.

This study examines incompressible polar active liquids containing quenched disorder across dimensions where $d > 2$. We analyze both linear and nonlinear responses within a Mean-field framework, finding that a flow induced by a linear force exhibits a saturation behavior at large magnitudes, characterized by a specific volume velocity. In contrast, no such limit volume velocity exists for velocities induced by linear rotation. The inclusion of quenched quenched disorder increases the coefficient of friction in the steady state, enhancing linearity without altering the existence of saturation. Supporting these theoretical predictions, we outline experimental and numerical approaches to probe such phenomena, ultimately connecting these results to potential applications in swarm dynamics.

Evading fraud involving misleading information in National Identity Cards requires quickly and accurately reading the card data. Evaluations using 200 images with 400 instances of digit fields demonstrate that OCR alone reaches 99.5% accuracy. Furthermore, integrating NLNA improves the precision of name and address fields significantly, achieving 100% accuracy for name detection and 99% for address detection.

Specifically, given a regular strategy as input, the proposed algorithm produces equivalent deterministic first-order formulas in the MS0 logic (without counting operators) and deterministic automata constrained by state transitions defined by computable functions.

Attractor identification and comparison serve as essential steps in analyzing the qualitative behavior of dynamical systems of differential equations. In this work, we present algorithms tasked with identifying such "wildcard" attractors by identifying a path in the state space leading to states exhibiting distinct dynamical behavior from previously known attractors. These proposed techniques are demonstrated within a range of significant biological and chemical models, with applications extending from diseases like HIV and influenza to patterns of excitement in cardiac tissues.

(2006, ApJ, 660, 1033) algorithm systematically alter $E_B$. The analysis reveals that signal noise levels and imaging field-of-view limitations can induce $E_B$ values significantly deviating from zero and negatively impact its overall measurement accuracy. Ultimately, these findings provide a quantitative framework for identifying and mitigating biased errors within these inferred solar magnetic field components.

The sign problem constitutes one of the most formidable challenges in quantum simulation via quantum Monte Carlo methods. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the ansatz exhibits optimal scaling with respect to both system volume and particle count. Our findings provide a much-needed advancement for large-scale, particle-rich systems that were previously inaccessible due to the severity of the sign problem.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has established itself as the primary method for advancing large language models (LLMs), yet it requires substantial and expensive datasets for each individual task—a bottleneck that RLHF alone cannot overcome. This paper introduces RETGAR, a novel, lightweight approach that enables pairwise-typed generalization from single-task feedback to multi-task scenarios. Given a seed task with an existing labeled dataset, RETHF automatically generates further tasks and acquires data point labels using few-shot techniques and intrinsic feedback signals. Our experiments demonstrate that RETGAR effectively enhances model performance across diverse domains including summarization, question answering, machine translation, and information retrieval.

Optimizing both hyperparameters and private data learning together is a challenging task that has rarely been addressed with effective methods before. We introduce DPO, the first differential private framework designed for effective optimization of deep learning hyperparameters with two main innovations: it treats the search for ideal hyperparameters as a stochastic process within a simulated training environment, avoiding the privacy costs of differential privacy on actual data, and it applies private stochastic gradient descent to ensure the learned model hyperparameters remain differentially private with respect to the training dataset. We validated DPO across several different deep learning architectures, architectures, and scenarios, finding that it outperformed existing methods in efficiency and achieved higher model accuracy after optimization, with the added benefit that search effort scales significantly as the number of candidate hyperparameter sets grows.

The loss function represents the core of a deep learning model, effectively guiding network learning and parameter optimization through its design. Nevertheless, the prevalence of empirical loss functions composed via trial and error suggests that theoretical investigations into their impact on deep classification models are crucial but underdeveloped. This paper offers a systematic analysis of classification loss functions for deep neural networks, outlining and evaluating various optimization metrics and their underlying properties to clarify their procedures and contexts. Recognizing that theoretical benchmarks are often unavailable for modern, complex deep models, this study introduces significant innovations in benchmark construction: first, a unified framework applied to homogeneous datasets, and second, a new cross-dataset evaluation method applicable to heterogeneous data. These prescribed evaluations, when combined with analyses of generalization and parameter dynamics, reveal distinct influence patterns of different loss functions across diverse deep neural networks. specifically, researcher-specific choices in loss function adoption appear to introduce parameter optimizations sufficient to affect model performance outcomes.

The following work focuses on the thermomechanical analysis of polymer chain dynamics during the crystallization process triggered by both stress and heat. This phenomenon is notably prevalent in semi-crystalline polymeric materials, which exhibit a distinct lack of long-range molecular order. Our investigation employs the finite element framework in conjunction with constitutive models tailored for such strains. This approach enables the integration of crystal nucleation and growth mechanisms within a series of complex one and multi-dimensional simulations of finite parts made from these materials. These models are constructed to assess how crystal formation influences stress, temperature, and material deformation across the system. The study examines the impact of heat generation due to crystallization and stress-induced crystallomorphology on the resulting microstructural patterns. Key findings demonstrate that heat generation and stress-oriented crystallization growth markedly influence the final morphology. Specifically, crystallomorphological outcomes are highly sensitive to whether glass transition effects are included in the analysis. We observe that temperature-dependent nucleation and growth rates are essential for accurate prediction. Furthermore, we confirm that nucleation and crystal growth follow an anisotropic orientation with respect to the active principal strain direction. This study provides insights into the microstructural development of stress-and-temperature triggered crystallization in polymers. Such knowledge holds utility for interpreting various real-world scenarios involving semi-crystalline polymer behavior.

This study examines a doped Bi$_2$Se$_{2}$ topological insulator exhibiting superconducting phases susceptible to perturbations from both magnetic fields and lattice deformations. We analyze the responses to an external magnetic field within the $\text{C}-\text{phase}$, a triplet superconducting stage characterized by an anisotropy along the c-axis and a Fermi surface shift, commonly explained by nematicity. Our computational results demonstrate that, for sufficiently strong lattice symmetry breaking, the magnetization arises from both band and carrier contributions, with Pauli paramagnetism being the dominant effect under typical experimental conditions. Furthermore, we observe a pronounced enhancement in susceptibility due to the rearrangement of electronic states near the Zezer split energy levels. Ultimately, we acknowledge the limitations regarding our understanding of the material's underlying superconducting mechanisms and experimental context.

We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive collection of 2,000 open-ended verification inquiries designed to evaluate if-then reasoning capability in closed-form mathematical problems. ATOMIC distinguishes itself through a stringent approval process involving four distinct roles—writer, verifier, approver, and master verifier—each relying solely yes/no answers to ensure rigorous quality control without the leakage of specific solutions. Our evaluation analysis of 2,000 approved inquiries reveals nuanced patterns across various subtopics within mathematically rigorous inquiries. ATOMIC features illustrative written solutions for each query alongside a series of handcrafted logical counterexamples. Demonstrations utilizing these high-quality structured resources indicate that advanced large language models achieve approximately 60% accuracy, while baseline trainable generative benchmarks struggle significantly, managing less than 5% success on this task.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SOPE) involves inducing a significant spin-orbit interaction across an material due to a neighboring layer with strong internal spin-orbit coupling; this phenomenon is essential for developing novel devices in the field of spin electronics. Within transition metal bismuth (Bi/Co) stacks, growing literature highlights how varying interfaces influence SOPE and resistance anisotropy, yet clarifying the specific mechanisms linking these outcomes remains challenging. Leveraging magneto-transport measurements, X-ray structural analysis, and first-principles simulations, we demonstrate that modifying the crystalline coherence between Bi and Co alters both the magnitude of spin-orbit resistance anisotropy in cobalt and the spatial extent of the SOPE originating from the bicoble. Disordered connective layers are found to suppress spin diffusion across the interface while simultaneously reducing resistance anisotropy and SOPE strength within the coboble. Consequently, this work establishes that suppressed spin diffusion, not just short atomic order, constrains the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect.

This paper presents partial regression inference methods for utilizing network data when analyzing networks with extensive populations. The framework allows for the estimation of network endogenous variables through network adjacency matrices, covering a spectrum from binary indicators to continuous scale from -1 to 1. We estimate standard errors that account for network data specificity, ensuring asymptotic normality across various sampling methods by using heteroskedasticity-consistent variance estimators. In network analysis applications, our method involves a three-step process: first, the model is fitted; second, coefficients are rounded to the nearest 0.05 to mitigate multiple correlation issues and enhance estimation stability of the remaining uncorrelated variables; finally, coefficients are ordered by their standard for significance comparison. To demonstrate the approach, we analyze the standard for network peer influences using US high school data. The results indicate that in this context, face-to-face interactions carry a heavier standard influence than participation in the same extracurricular activities.

We introduce a framework for structured, free-form textual dialogue designed to teach conversationally autonomous agents theory-of-mind (ToM). This system defines a hierarchy of text generation intents, requiring agents to explicitly state their planned action before executing it. We demonstrate that Hierarchy of Intents ToM significantly enhances dialogue coherence and duration in common testing scenarios compared to standard unconstrained text generation. Furthermore, we introduce a "Markov Canvas"—a novel data representation for conversations—to visually compare different generation strategies and identify the mechanisms driving increased talkativeness. These visual advances offer a potential remedy for the issue where advanced language models produce verbose but circular responses, colloquially known as "talking about the same things over and over again."

Knotted proteins serve as a vital model for investigating folding mechanics through a selection strategy based on bending pathways derived from native states. Although previous research utilized geometric measures to identify these pathways from contact maps—thereby providing an efficient method to detect knots in sequences with long cyclic permutations—those approaches require refinement for the specific study of protein folding routes. Consequently, an alternative selection criterion employing a new topological measure is proposed to characterize bending pathways and their associated transitions. While preserving the efficiency of contact map utilization, this new selection is designed to offer a more rigorous representation and detection of the geometric features inherent within knotted protein structures.

The Nambu-Goldstone theorem establishes a connection between certain broken continuous symmetries and the existence of massless particles known as Nambu-Goldstone bosons. This relationship generally fails to arise within soliton solutions or solutions exhibiting topological symmetry breaking. Using a rigorous mathematical treatment of the particle concept within relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, we demonstrate specifically how the theorem breaks down when central extensions occur within the symmetry algebra. Furthermore, we explicitly construct an example featuring the Cremer mode within a massive $\phi^4$ field theory that features $O(N)$ symmetry; in this case, the specified four-colloidal solution exhibits broken global symmetries across all its internal degrees of freedom, yet no Nambu-Goldstone bosons are present in the spectrum relative to this state.

Remote epitaxy on trigonal substrates, such as 6H-SiC and sapphire, is a nasned approach for manufacturing high-performance heterostructures. The primary challenge lies in achieving single-crystalline growth, as the competing interests between the pinhole and van der Waals modes typically favor a mixed equilibrium at standard deposition conditions. Using synchrotron X-ray diffraction, this study investigates the film-fabrication of Heusler alloys—specifically the ferromagnetic Pt-doped (Pt-doped) and paramagnetic Ni-doped (Ni-doped) variants—on graphene-sapphire systems. The results reveal a distinct transition: on a paramagnetic substrate, the system shifts to van der Waals mode deposition, characterized by an abrupt shift in lattice offset to match substrate planes; conversely, at ferromagnetic alignment, growth transitions to remote epitopy, defined by a lattice offset equal to zero. This shift appears driven primarily by differential thermal expansion coefficients, which modify interfacial stresses, an effect most pronounced at elevated temperatures. These findings offer crucial insights for predicting and managing epitaxial modes during the fabrication of strain-sensitive heterostructures on remote epitaxy platforms.

Heart sound classification is emerging as an important step in diagnosing cardiac disorders, yet these signals remain highly susceptible to environmental and physiological disruptions such as additive noise and convolutioanal distortion. This study presents a classification method tailored for noisy heart sounds that employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), utilizing specific architectures to handle both types of interference. To address additive noise, we trained and evaluated the model on datasets augmented with noise levels matching those found in genuine recordings. For convolutioanal distortion, which prevents standard preprocessing techniques like envelope extraction and filtering, we used an approach designed to preserve the spatial integrity of the representations. We assessed performance across three distinct scenarios involving varying additive noise intensities and convolutioanal distortion levels; in each case, the proposed framework achieved state-of-the-art results, demonstrating that accurate classification of heart sound categories is feasible despite simultaneous presence of both distortions.

In the realm of wearable health, enabling models to perform specific diagnostic tasks while maintaining strict user privacy and data security is increasingly important. Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution for these private data challenges, yet it often requires retraining with access to the target device's data distribution—a step that conflicts with user confidentiality and is frequently impractical. We introduce FedHealth, an innovative federated transfer knowledge framework that facilitates model deployment on wearables without needing their data distributions for training. Our approach transfers knowledge from the source health task adaptation to the new (target) one, ensuring efficient learning on-device. To execute this without compromising privacy, we employ a dual mechanism: first, a knowledgeloss measurement quantifies the impact of any transfer, and the magnitude of this metric dictates the subsequent step. Second, if the metric indicates a significant impact, it triggers federated fine-tuning, which allows uniform adjustment across different devices using encrypted data uploads and knowledge-optimized parameters. Conversely, if the impact is minor, the knowledge is directly integrated into the target task. Our assessments on three distinct datasets demonstrates that our method maintains high knowledge transfer efficiency and achieves competitive predictive accuracy across multiple use cases.

This study examines various methods of portfolio optimization grounded in higher moments and provides comparisons with existing approaches. We offer formulations for portfolio optimization by incorporating skewness and kurtosis, addressing both localized and global market equilibria in accordance with von Neumann's Nash equilibrium principles. Additionally, in a non-locally balanced environment, we explore the higher moment-based reallocation strategy known as the CPPR rule, deriving an explicit expression for this component. Our findings serve as a foundational reference for future research investigating multi-variable optimization problems within portfolio contexts.

Software that has previously required manual handling faces numerous obstacles when processed by standard automated methods. To address this, I introduced the concept of Self-Improving Automated Software (SIA), designed to overcome such barriers through escalating simplification across multiple passes. An SIA system transforms a specific input instance into an training example; subsequently, the system utilizes these examples to improve its ability to process similar data in the future. While current approaches rely on reinforcement learning or supervised learning, my approach is novel and fully unsupervised. Although generalizations remain limited, the core methodology offers a distinct unsupervised paradigm. My experimental focus centers on automatically processing birth certificates—a complex document type historically difficult to handle without manual intervention. My unsupervised system successfully processes this task with an accuracy of 97.3%, a significant rise from baseline levels of approximately 83%, representing an eight-certificate-per-thousand decrease in error, which could save entities like insurance firms millions of dollars and countless hours each year.

We introduce DNAUp, a practical file system for DNA storage that effectively addresses two critical challenges in current research: representing hierarchical directory structures and executing file updates. Most existing DNA storage methods flatten the file system, merging directories with data; while this avoids the costly random access associated with native DNA access patterns, it compromises the reliability of restored data due to inherent storage errors. Such flattening works well for raw data archival, but is inappropriate for programs processing web content, media files, and other easily corrupted information. In DNAUp, directory names and file data are encoded separately, enabling targeted random access to both via distinct synthesis orders. The system employs efficient data structures to manage DNA storage updates by leveraging local access characteristics and minimizing redundant writing. We evaluated DNAUp through a realistic tracerbed simulation and compare key metrics against a state-of-the-art modern DNA storage solution.

Standard diffusion is typified by a normal distribution of particle displacements where the variance increases linearly over time. In contrast, anomalous diffusion involves deviations from normality, characterized by variances that scale as $t^\alpha$ ($\alpha \neq 1$), and frequently appears in biological contexts such as intracellular movement. Although standard diffusion-advected equations are derived from a constant diffusivity, anomalous diffusion typically results from time-dependent or spatial-varied diffusivities; however, explicit general solutions for these scenarios have eluded derivation. This study presents exact solutions for three distinct mechanisms producing anomalous diffusion: diffusivities that fluctuate randomly over time, fluctuate based on position, or respond to local historical positions. These solutions correspond to specific fractional-order advection-diffusion equation scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate that diffusion under random time-dependent parameters (yielding Levy stable distributions with scaling exponents $\< 1$) satisfies the fractional equation, while two particular cases—diffusivities dictated by random spatial variables and those responding to past positioning—satisfy fractional equations characterized by integer-stabilized components and result in Gaussian particle distributions.

Imitation learning, supervised by expert demonstrations, has proven highly effective in training intelligent agents; however, acquiring these demonstrations is often costly and labor-intensive. The peer distribution in our framework function so that each agent acts not only as an explorer but also as an instructor, enabling simultaneous experience gathering and knowledge acquisition. Mathematical analysis within our study confirms the validity of our method, and extensive experiments across five distinct environments substantiate that SID delivers considerable performance gains compared to current state-of-the-art methods in practical applications.

Using a dynamic model that adds a competitive element to the standard endogenous mobility cycle, this study examines whether rising upward movement automatically leads to better equal chances for advancement. This paper examines a quantized, distributed optimization framework operating under malicious attacks. Annotation correction is crucial for maintaining high-quality datasets used in machine learning tasks. We utilize various BERT components to assist in identifying and correcting errors within this specific domain: detecting mismatches via predicted label probabilities between questions asserting unknown information and those with specific answers; verifying factual consistency between the question content and their claimed responses; and evaluating semantic similarity between distinct pairs of labeled datasets. We conduct experiments on a political dataset to demonstrate that having BERT guide annotation refinement improves classification model accuracy and F1 scores compared to using uncorrected data with non-expert annotations, highlighting the method's effectiveness in this domain.
